title: Moroccan Couscous with Seven Vegetables
subtitle: A traditional North African feast of couscous and slow-cooked vegetables
excerpt: Seven-vegetable couscous is a celebratory dish served at Moroccan family tables for Friday gatherings and special occasions. A fragrant stew of root vegetables, courgette, butternut squash, and chickpeas is ladled over light, fluffy couscous and eaten communally from a large shared platter. The seven vegetables are symbolic; the exact combination varies by household and season.
sourceNotes: Couscous is one of the oldest and most culturally significant dishes of North Africa, with roots stretching back to the Berber communities of the Maghreb. Seven-vegetable couscous is a particularly celebrated version associated with Moroccan family cooking, where the number seven carries cultural and spiritual significance.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The vegetable stew can be made up to 2 days ahead and reheated. Steam or rehydrate the couscous fresh.
recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the vegetable stew only, not the couscous. Reheat and serve over freshly made couscous.

content.text: This dish is far simpler than its celebratory reputation suggests. The vegetable stew comes together in a single large pot; the couscous is rehydrated in minutes with boiling water or stock. Add the courgette and squash later in the cooking time than the root vegetables so nothing goes mushy. Although it is labelled gluten-free here for the stew, standard couscous is made from wheat: use millet or rice couscous if you need the whole dish to be gluten-free.

content.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, wide saucepan over medium heat. Add the sliced onions and cook for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until softened and beginning to turn golden at the edges.
Add the ground cumin, coriander, cinnamon, and turmeric. Stir for 1 minute until the spices are fragrant and coating the onions.
Add the tinned tomatoes and vegetable stock. Stir well and season generously with salt and pepper. Bring to a simmer.
Add the carrots, parsnips, and potatoes. These are the hardest vegetables and need the most time. Bring back to a simmer, cover, and cook over low heat for 20 minutes.

Add the butternut squash, courgette, and drained chickpeas. Replace the lid and cook for a further 20 to 25 minutes until all the vegetables are tender but holding their shape. Taste and adjust seasoning.

While the stew finishes, prepare the couscous. Place the couscous in a large heatproof bowl. Pour over 480ml of boiling water or hot stock and a pinch of salt. Stir once, cover with a plate or cling film, and leave for 5 minutes.
Fluff the couscous with a fork to separate the grains. Mound it on a large serving platter. Ladle the vegetable stew over the top, scatter with fresh coriander, and serve immediately.

items.symptom: The couscous is lumpy and clumped
items.cause: The couscous was not fluffed straight after rehydrating, allowing the grains to stick together as they cooled.
items.fix: Fluff immediately after the 5-minute resting time while still warm. If already clumped, rub the couscous gently between your palms to break apart the clumps, then fluff with a fork. A small knob of butter or drizzle of olive oil stirred through also helps separate the grains.

items.symptom: The vegetables have all turned to mush
items.cause: The courgette and squash were added at the same time as the root vegetables and had too long to cook.
items.fix: Always add soft vegetables like courgette in the final 20 minutes of cooking. Root vegetables need the full 40 to 45 minutes; courgette needs no more than 15 to 20. If the stew is already overcooked, serve as-is: it will still taste good, even if the texture is softer than ideal.

items.symptom: The stew is thin and watery
items.cause: Too much stock was added, or the lid stayed on the whole time so nothing reduced.
items.fix: Remove the lid for the final 10 to 15 minutes to allow some liquid to evaporate and the sauce to thicken. A small amount of tomato paste stirred in early helps build body. Next time, start with slightly less stock and add more if needed.
